opus-5.5.text:
I think it came from a pretty honest realization that I wasn't the kind of person who could just glance at something and immediately get it. Some people around me seemed to absorb new material really quickly, and for a while that made me anxious. But at some point I accepted that I simply needed more time, and instead of fighting that, I tried to build my approach around it.

So practically, that meant starting early. If there was something I knew I'd need, whether it was a course topic, a programming skill, or a research area, I'd try to get exposure to it well before I actually had to use it. That way, when the pressure came, I wasn't learning from zero. I'd already gone through the confusing phase on my own schedule.

It also changed how I learned. I became much more hands-on. Reading something or listening to a lecture never really stuck for me until I'd implemented it myself, broken it, and fixed it again. That's slower in the short term, but the understanding is much deeper, and it compounds. A lot of the work I ended up doing, especially building tools and infrastructure, came out of that habit of wanting to really understand how things work by building them.

And honestly, it made me more patient with myself. I stopped measuring myself against how fast other people were going and focused more on whether I was steadily making progress. If you keep showing up and putting in the time consistently, over a few years the gap closes, and sometimes you end up further ahead than you expected.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention sleeping or being able to recite material fluently afterward.

r002.rationale: It says she started early and learned material before she needed it, but does not say she started earlier than other students.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think I figured out pretty early that I wasn't the kind of person who could glance at something once and have it click. In high school, and later at Tsinghua, I'd watch classmates pick up a concept in a lecture and move on, and I'd still be sitting there turning it over. For a while that bothered me. Then I kind of accepted it, and that acceptance changed how I worked.

The first thing it did was make me start earlier. If I knew a topic would take me longer, I couldn't afford to wait until the week before an exam or a deadline. So I'd front-load. I'd read ahead before the lecture, so that when the professor explained it, it was my second pass instead of my first. That alone made a huge difference, because the lecture stopped being the place where I had to understand everything and became more like a check on what I'd already struggled with.

The second thing is that I leaned heavily on building things instead of just reading. For me, reading a paper or a textbook chapter is kind of a false sense of understanding. I'd nod along and then realize I couldn't reproduce it. So I'd write the code. For reinforcement learning especially, that's how Tianshou started. I wanted to actually understand the algorithms, and the only way I trusted myself to understand them was to implement them, get them wrong, debug them, and see the learning curves come out right. That's slow, but the understanding sticks in a way that reading never did for me.

And the third thing, I'd say, is that I got comfortable asking what felt like dumb questions, and asking them early. If you need more time anyway, you can't also waste time being stuck quietly out of pride. I'd go to office hours, I'd message people, I'd post in forums. Most of the time the thing I was stuck on was something small that someone could clear up in two minutes, and then I'd get my time back.

So I guess the short version is: knowing I was slower made me more deliberate. It pushed me toward depth over breadth, toward doing rather than consuming, and toward being honest about what I didn't know. Looking back, I don't think it was a disadvantage. It just forced good habits on me that some faster people never had to develop.

r002.rationale: She says needing longer led her to start earlier, front-load studying, and read ahead before lectures; the contrast with classmates who picked things up in lecture supports the comparison.

It also meant starting earlier, because I didn’t want to feel rushed. Instead of judging myself by how quickly I could learn something, I focused more on whether I really understood it.
